claim: Atg1 kinase is essential for autophagy in Schizosaccharomyces pombe.
source: Using an mYFP-Atg8 processing assay, which monitors the autophagy-dependent release of free mYFP upon the processing of mYFP-Atg8 by vacuolar proteases, we found that both mutations abolished nitrogen starvation-induced autophagy (Figure 1A), suggesting that like in S. cerevisiae, the kinase activity of Atg1 is essential for autophagy in S. pombe.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the mYFP-Atg8 processing assay showing that kinase-inactivating mutations (D193A and T208A) abolished autophagy, and by comparison to established knowledge in S. cerevisiae.

claim: D193A and T208A mutations abolish the kinase activity of S. pombe Atg1.
source: When endogenously mCherry-tagged Atg1 was immunopurified from cells grown under nutrient-rich conditions and subjected to this in vitro kinase assay, an immunoblotting band reactive to the anti-thioP antibody was observed at a position overlapping the top edge of the mCherry-antibody-reactive band (Figure 1C), suggesting that Atg1 underwent in vitro autophosphorylation. Such a band was not observed for D193A and T208A mutants, confirming that they are indeed kinase dead (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data showing absence of autophosphorylation signal for these mutants.

claim: In S. pombe, Atg11 but not Atg13, Atg17, or Atg101 is required for Atg1 kinase activity.
source: Surprisingly, we found that in S. pombe, Atg1 from atg13Δ, atg17Δ, or atg101Δ mutant exhibited autophosphorylation activities similar to that of Atg1 from wild type, under both nutrient-rich and nitrogen-starved conditions (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A). By contrast, the in vitro autophosphorylation activity of Atg1 from atg11Δ mutant was almost undetectable (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data comparing Atg1 activity from different deletion mutants.

claim: Atg1 is phosphorylated in vivo in wild type but not in atg11Δ mutant.
source: Treating immunopurified Atg1 with lambda protein phosphatase did not alter the migration of Atg1 from atg11Δ mutant, but rendered Atg1 from wild type migrating as fast as Atg1 from atg11Δ mutant (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that Atg1 is phosphorylated in vivo in wild type but not in atg11Δ mutant.
evidence: The claim is supported by phosphatase treatment experiments showing differential migration patterns.

claim: Atg11 is required for Atg1 kinase activity toward non-self substrates.
source: Peptide S but not peptide A was phosphorylated by Atg1 immunopurified from wild type (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D). By contrast, Atg1 immunopurified from atg11Δ mutant failed to phosphorylate peptide S (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D). Thus, Atg11 is required for Atg1 kinase activities toward not only itself but also a non-self substrate.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data using peptide S as a non-self substrate.

claim: Atg11(522-583) is necessary and sufficient for the autophagy function of Atg11.
source: In the mYFP-Atg8 processing assay, Atg11(522-583)Δ, which lacks these 62 residues, failed to rescue atg11Δ (Figure 1F). By contrast, Atg11(522-583) rescued atg11Δ as well as full-length Atg11 (Figure 1F). Similar results were obtained using the Pho8Δ60 assay, where we expressed the autophagy reporter S. cerevisiae Pho8Δ60 in S. pombe pho8Δ background (Yu et al., 2020; Figure 1G). These results show that Atg11(522-583) is necessary and sufficient for the autophagy function of Atg11.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from mYFP-Atg8 processing assay and Pho8Δ60 assay, and cites previous work by Yu et al., 2020.

claim: Atg11(522-583) is necessary and sufficient for the ability of Atg11 to support Atg1 kinase activity.
source: Atg11(522-583), when expressed in atg11Δ, rescued the loss of the Atg1 kinase activity toward itself and peptide S, whereas Atg11(522-583)Δ failed to rescue (Figure 1H). Thus, Atg11(522-583) is necessary and sufficient for the ability of Atg11 to support the Atg1 kinase activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data showing rescue of Atg1 activity by Atg11(522-583).

claim: Under the conditions used, Atg11 is the only strong physical interactor of Atg1 among core Atg proteins.
source: Consistent with this idea, in an affinity purification coupled with mass spectrometry (AP-MS) analysis using Atg1 as bait, we were only able to detect Atg1 and Atg11 but not any other core Atg proteins (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that, under the conditions we used, Atg11 is the only strong physical interactor of Atg1 among core Atg proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by AP-MS experimental data and is explicitly qualified by the experimental conditions.

claim: Atg11 physically interacts with Atg1.
source: We confirmed the Atg1-Atg11 interaction by coimmunoprecipitation using endogenously tagged proteins (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by coimmunoprecipitation experimental data.

claim: Atg11(522-583) interacts with the tMIT domain of Atg1.
source: Using this assay, we found that Atg11(522-583) interacted with the C-terminal tandem MIT (tMIT) domain of Atg1 but not with the N-terminal kinase domain or the disordered region situated between the kinase domain and the tMIT domain (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Pil1 co-tethering assay data.

claim: The N-terminal 10 amino acids of Atg11(522-583) are required for Atg1 binding.
source: Upon further truncation, we found that Atg11(522-552) but not Atg11(532-583) interacted with the tMIT domain of Atg1 (Figure 2C). Thus, the N-terminal 10 amino acids of Atg11(522-583) are required for Atg1 binding.
evidence: The claim is supported by Pil1 co-tethering assay data with truncated Atg11 fragments.

claim: Atg11(522-544) is sufficient for interacting with Atg1.
source: Using the yeast two-hybrid (Y2H) assay, we narrowed down the Atg1-interacting region of Atg11 to Atg11(522-544) (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Y2H assay data.

claim: F526 and Y527 are conserved aromatic residues in Atg11 from multiple fission yeast species.
source: Based on an alignment of Atg11 from multiple fission yeast species, we identified two conserved aromatic residues in the β-strand section: F526 and Y527 (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data across multiple species.

claim: Mutating either F526 or Y527 to alanine abolishes the autophagy function of Atg11(522-583).
source: mYFP-Atg8 processing assay showed that either F526 or Y527, when mutated to alanine, abolished the autophagy function of Atg11(522-583) (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by mYFP-Atg8 processing assay data with point mutants.

claim: Atg11(522-544) directly interacts with the tMIT domain of Atg1 in a manner dependent on F526 and Y527.
source: Using recombinant proteins purified from E. coli to perform in vitro pull-down assays, we found that Atg11(522-544) directly interacted with the tMIT domain of Atg1 in a manner dependent on F526 and Y527 (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro pull-down assay data using recombinant proteins.

claim: The interaction between Atg11(522-544) and Atg1 is required for the autophagy function of Atg11(522-583).
source: Together, these results show that Atg11(522-544) mediates a specific and direct interaction with Atg1, and this interaction is required for the autophagy function of Atg11(522-583).
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from multiple experimental results showing that mutations disrupting the interaction also disrupt autophagy function.

claim: Atg1 binding is not the only function of Atg11(522-583).
source: Atg11(522-552), a fragment sufficient for Atg1 binding, cannot support autophagy (Figure 1E), suggesting that Atg1 binding is not the only function of Atg11(522-583).
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing that Atg11(522-552) binds Atg1 but cannot rescue autophagy.

claim: Both Atg11(522-583) and full-length Atg11 can self-interact.
source: Using a coimmunoprecipitation assay, we found that both Atg11(522-583) and full-length Atg11 can self-interact (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by coimmunoprecipitation assay data.

claim: Atg11(546-583) but not Atg11(522-552) is able to self-interact.
source: Using further truncated fragments to perform coimmunoprecipitation analysis, we found that Atg11(546-583) but not Atg11(522-552) was able to self-interact (Figure 3B and C). These results were corroborated by the Y2H assay (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by coimmunoprecipitation and Y2H assay data.

claim: Atg11(522-583) forms a homodimer.
source: MBP-Atg11(522-583) eluted at an elution volume corresponding to that of a 101.8 kD protein. Because MBP-Atg11(522-583) has a calculated molecular weight of 50.6 kD, we concluded that Atg11(522-583) forms a homodimer.
evidence: The claim is supported by gel filtration chromatography data comparing elution volumes to molecular weight standards.

claim: Atg11(546-583)-mediated dimerization is essential for the normal functions of Atg11.
source: This internal deletion disrupted the self-interaction of Atg11 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), abolished the autophagy function of Atg11 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), and abrogated the ability of Atg11 to support the Atg1 kinase activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D). Thus, Atg11(546-583)-mediated dimerization is essential for the normal functions of Atg11.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from multiple assays showing loss of function when the dimerization domain is deleted.

claim: Dimerization is the main function of the C-terminal part of Atg11(522-583).
source: We fused a 32-amino-acid-long homodimerizing leucine zipper motif (LZ) (Luo et al., 2015) to Atg11 fragments and examined the ability of the fusion proteins to complement the autophagy phenotype of atg11Δ. LZ fusion fully restored the ability of Atg11(522-552) to complement atg11Δ (Figure 3F and G). Thus, dimerization is the main function of the C-terminal part of Atg11(522-583).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional complementation data showing that a heterologous dimerization domain can replace the native dimerization domain, and cites Luo et al., 2015.

claim: Atg11(522-583) is composed of two separable functional modules: an Atg1-binding domain and a homodimerization domain.
source: Together, our results demonstrate that Atg11(522-583) is composed of two separable functional modules, an Atg1-binding domain and a homodimerization domain.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experiments showing that the N-terminal region binds Atg1 and the C-terminal region mediates dimerization, and these functions can be separated.

claim: ER stress-induced ER-phagy requires Atg11 in S. pombe.
source: When cells were treated with the ER stress inducer dithiothreitol (DTT), processing of Erg11-CFP occurred in a manner dependent on the ER-phagy receptor Epr1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Zhao et al., 2020). DTT-induced processing of Erg11 was blocked in atg11Δ cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), indicating that, like bulk autophagy, ER stress-induced selective ER-phagy also requires Atg11.
evidence: The claim is supported by Erg11-CFP processing assay data and cites Zhao et al., 2020.

claim: Atg11(522-583) can support ER stress-induced selective ER-phagy.
source: Interestingly, the ER-phagy defect of atg11Δ can be rescued by Atg11(522-583) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2). Thus, this 62 amino acid fragment of Atg11, even though lacking the region involved in autophagy receptor binding in other organisms, can support a selective autophagy pathway in S. pombe.
evidence: The claim is supported by Erg11-CFP processing assay data showing rescue by Atg11(522-583).

claim: The dimerization ability of Atg11 is important for supporting selective autophagy.
source: Moreover, we found that Atg11(522-552)-LZ but not Atg11(522-552) can rescue the ER-phagy defect of atg11Δ (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), indicating that the dimerization ability of Atg11 is important for supporting selective autophagy.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that adding a dimerization domain restores ER-phagy function.

claim: Artificial dimerization of Atg1 can bypass the requirement of Atg11 for autophagy.
source: This fusion protein, Atg1-LZ, but not wild-type Atg1, rescued the autophagy defect of atg1Δ atg11Δ double deletion mutant (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by mYFP-Atg8 processing assay data showing rescue by Atg1-LZ.

claim: Artificial dimerization of Atg1 can bypass the requirement of Atg11 for Atg1 kinase activity.
source: Furthermore, Atg1-LZ but not Atg1 immunopurified from atg1Δ atg11Δ cells exhibited robust in vitro autophosphorylation activity (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data.

claim: The main role of Atg11 is to dimerize Atg1, thereby causing Atg1 activation.
source: Thus, Atg11 is no longer needed when Atg1 is conferred an ability to homodimerize, supporting the idea that the main role of Atg11 is to dimerize Atg1, and thereby cause Atg1 activation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing that artificial dimerization of Atg1 bypasses the need for Atg11.

claim: Atg1 activation can occur when activation by trans-autophosphorylation is no longer possible.
source: Interestingly, this rescue was not affected when the kinase-dead mutations D193A and T208A were introduced into Atg1-GBP or Atg1-GFP and was only abolished when both Atg1-GFP and Atg1-GBP harbored kinase-dead mutations (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B). These results indicate that Atg1 activation can still occur when activation by trans-autophosphorylation is no longer possible (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from GFP-GBP heterodimerization experiments showing that only one active kinase in a dimer is sufficient.

claim: Atg1 can be activated by dimerization-induced cis-autophosphorylation.
source: Thus, we conclude that Atg1 can be activated by dimerization-induced cis-autophosphorylation (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is concluded from experimental data showing that one active kinase in a dimer is sufficient for activation.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, Atg13 and Atg17 are required for activating Atg1 kinase during nitrogen starvation-induced non-selective bulk autophagy.
source: In S. cerevisiae, two scaffold proteins Atg13 and Atg17 are required for activating Atg1 kinase during nitrogen starvation-induced non-selective bulk autophagy (Kamada et al., 2000; Yeh et al., 2010; Yeh et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kamada et al., 2000; Yeh et al., 2010; Yeh et al., 2011.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, during bulk autophagy, monomeric Atg13 makes multivalent interactions with dimeric Atg17, generating supramolecular assemblies that allow concentration-dependent Atg1 autophosphorylation and autoactivation.
source: In this Atg1 activation mode, monomeric Atg13, which can directly bind Atg1, makes multivalent interactions with dimeric Atg17, and thereby generates supramolecular assemblies, allowing concentration-dependent Atg1 autophosphorylation and autoactivation (Yeh et al., 2011; Fujioka et al., 2014; Yamamoto et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yeh et al., 2011; Fujioka et al., 2014; Yamamoto et al., 2016.

claim: In S. cerevisiae Cvt pathway, Atg17 is dispensable but Atg13 and Atg11 are required for Atg1 activation.
source: The cytoplasm-to-vacuole targeting (Cvt) pathway in S. cerevisiae, a selective autophagy pathway that operates under nutrient-rich conditions, employs a different Atg1 activation mechanism where Atg17 is dispensable but Atg13 and another scaffold protein Atg11 are required (Kamada et al., 2000; Kim et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kamada et al., 2000; Kim et al., 2001.

claim: In S. cerevisiae Cvt pathway, Atg11 tethers Atg1 to the multimeric cargo-receptor complex to promote Atg1 autophosphorylation and autoactivation.
source: In this Atg1 activation mode, Atg11 tethers Atg1 to the multimeric cargo-receptor complex to promote Atg1 autophosphorylation and autoactivation, and Atg13 plays a more indirect role by facilitating the Atg1-Atg11 interaction on the vacuole membrane (Kamber et al., 2015; Torggler et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kamber et al., 2015; Torggler et al., 2016.

claim: In mammals, FIP200/RB1CC1 is essential for bulk autophagy.
source: Unlike the situation in S. cerevisiae where Atg11 is dispensable for nitrogen starvation-induced bulk autophagy, in mammals, the Atg11-domain-harboring ortholog of S. cerevisiae Atg11, called FIP200 or RB1CC1, is essential for bulk autophagy (Hara et al., 2008; Ganley et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hara et al., 2008; Ganley et al., 2009.

claim: Atg11 orthologs in Drosophila melanogaster, Arabidopsis thaliana, Kluyveromyces marxianus, and Schizosaccharomyces pombe are indispensable for bulk autophagy.
source: Similarly, Atg11 orthologs in Drosophila melanogaster, Arabidopsis thaliana, and two yeast species Kluyveromyces marxianus and Schizosaccharomyces pombe are also indispensable for bulk autophagy (Kim et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2013; Li et al., 2014; Yamamoto et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2013; Li et al., 2014; Yamamoto et al., 2015.

claim: Mammalian and Drosophila Atg11/FIP200 proteins promote Atg1 kinase activity.
source: Mammalian and Drosophila Atg11/FIP200 proteins have been shown to promote Atg1 kinase activity (Ganley et al., 2009; Nagy et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ganley et al., 2009; Nagy et al., 2014.

claim: Atg11/FIP200 family proteins from diverse eukaryotic species can physically interact with Atg1.
source: Atg11/FIP200 proteins in diverse organisms can physically interact with Atg1 (Noda and Fujioka, 2015; Papinski and Kraft, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Noda and Fujioka, 2015; Papinski and Kraft, 2016.

claim: Self-interactions of Atg11/FIP200 proteins have been observed in S. cerevisiae, C. elegans, Arabidopsis, and mammals.
source: Self-interactions of Atg11/FIP200 proteins have been observed in S. cerevisiae (Kim et al., 2001; Yorimitsu and Klionsky, 2005), C. elegans (Lin et al., 2013), Arabidopsis (Li et al., 2014), and mammals (Turco et al., 2019; Shi et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2001; Yorimitsu and Klionsky, 2005; Lin et al., 2013; Li et al., 2014; Turco et al., 2019; Shi et al., 2020.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, Atg11 is required for bulk autophagy under carbon-depletion and phosphate-depletion conditions.
source: In S. cerevisiae, even though Atg11 is dispensable for nitrogen starvation-induced bulk autophagy (Kim et al., 2001), it is required for bulk autophagy under carbon-depletion and phosphate-depletion conditions (Adachi et al., 2017; Yokota et al., 2017), suggesting that S. cerevisiae Atg11 may also promote Atg1 activation independently of selective autophagy cargos and receptors under certain conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2001; Adachi et al., 2017; Yokota et al., 2017.

claim: Dimerization-induced cis-autophosphorylation is the activation mechanism for RAF, PKR, and RIPK3.
source: Dimerization-induced cis-autophosphorylation has been shown to be the activation mechanism for a small but increasing number of eukaryotic protein kinases including RAF, PKR, and RIPK3 (Hu et al., 2013; Dey et al., 2014; Raju et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hu et al., 2013; Dey et al., 2014; Raju et al., 2018.

claim: Atg11/FIP200 family proteins from diverse eukaryotic species share three annotated domains: a ubiquitin-like (Ubl) domain, an Atg17-like domain, and the Atg11 domain.
source: Atg11/FIP200 family proteins from diverse eukaryotic species including animals, fungi, amoebozoans, and plants all share three annotated domains: a ubiquitin-like (Ubl) domain (NCBI CDD cd17060), an Atg17-like domain (Pfam PF04108), and the hallmark Atg11 domain (Pfam PF10377; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by domain annotation data from NCBI CDD and Pfam databases.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, the C-terminal region of Atg11 is responsible for binding Atg19 and Atg32.
source: In S. cerevisiae, Atg11 promotes selective autophagy by directly interacting with selective autophagy receptors (Zientara-Rytter and Subramani, 2020). The C-terminal region of S. cerevisiae Atg11, which encompasses the conserved Atg11 domain, is responsible for binding Atg19 and Atg32, the autophagy receptors for the Cvt pathway and the mitophagy pathway, respectively (Yorimitsu and Klionsky, 2005; Aoki et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zientara-Rytter and Subramani, 2020; Yorimitsu and Klionsky, 2005; Aoki et al., 2011.

claim: FIP200 uses its Atg11-domain-containing C-terminal region to bind autophagy receptors CCPG1 and p62.
source: FIP200, the mammalian ortholog of Atg11, also uses its Atg11-domain-containing C-terminal region to bind autophagy receptors CCPG1 and p62 (Smith et al., 2018; Turco et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Smith et al., 2018; Turco et al., 2019.

claim: Atg11-mediated Atg1 activation may be a more ancient and more universal mechanism than the Atg17-dependent Atg1 activation mechanism.
source: Lending support to this idea is the fact that animals and plants have Atg11/FIP200 family proteins but do not have Atg17-like proteins (Li et al., 2014). Thus, Atg11-mediated Atg1 activation may be a more ancient and more universal mechanism than the Atg17-dependent Atg1 activation mechanism used by S. cerevisiae during nitrogen starvation-induced bulk autophagy.
evidence: The claim is speculative and inferred from phylogenetic distribution data, supported by citation to Li et al., 2014.

claim: Mediating Atg1 oligomerization and activation may be a conserved function of Atg11/FIP200 family proteins.
source: We propose that mediating Atg1 oligomerization and activation may be a conserved function of Atg11/FIP200 family proteins and cis-autophosphorylation may be a general mechanism of Atg1 activation.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the findings in S. pombe and evolutionary considerations.

claim: Cis-autophosphorylation may be a general mechanism of Atg1 activation.
source: We propose that mediating Atg1 oligomerization and activation may be a conserved function of Atg11/FIP200 family proteins and cis-autophosphorylation may be a general mechanism of Atg1 activation.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the findings in S. pombe.

claim: Atg1 is a serine/threonine kinase conserved across eukaryotes.
source: Atg proteins act in a hierarchical manner and among those acting most upstream is Atg1 (ULK1 in mammals), a serine/threonine kinase conserved across eukaryotes (Matsuura et al., 1997; Suzuki et al., 2007; Cheong et al., 2008; Noda and Fujioka, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Matsuura et al., 1997; Suzuki et al., 2007; Cheong et al., 2008; Noda and Fujioka, 2015.

claim: D193A and T208A mutations in S. pombe Atg1 are respectively the equivalents of the kinase-inactivating D211A and T226A mutations in S. cerevisiae Atg1.
source: To determine whether the kinase activity of S. pombe Atg1 is important for autophagy, we introduced D193A and T208A mutations individually into endogenously mCherry-tagged Atg1. These two mutations are respectively the equivalents of the kinase-inactivating D211A and T226A mutations in S. cerevisiae Atg1, with the former disrupting the chelation of a catalytic metal ion and the latter abolishing the activation loop phosphorylation site (Matsuura et al., 1997; Kijanska et al., 2010; Yeh et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to S. cerevisiae and citations to Matsuura et al., 1997; Kijanska et al., 2010; Yeh et al., 2010.

claim: Full-length Atg11 can self-interact independently of Atg1.
source: Coimmunoprecipitation assay showed that full-length Atg11 can self-interact independently of Atg1.
evidence: The claim is supported by coimmunoprecipitation data in atg1Δ cells shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Atg11(546-583)Δ cannot self-interact.
source: Coimmunoprecipitation assay showed that Atg11(546-583)Δ, which lacks the 38-amin-acid region (546-583) that mediates homodimerization, cannot self-interact.
evidence: The claim is supported by coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Atg11(546-583)Δ cannot rescue the autophagy defect of atg11Δ.
source: mYFP-Atg8 processing assay showed that Atg11(546-583)Δ cannot rescue the autophagy defect of atg11Δ.
evidence: The claim is supported by mYFP-Atg8 processing assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Atg11(546-583)Δ failed to support the kinase activity of Atg1.
source: Atg11(546-583)Δ failed to support the kinase activity of Atg1.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: ER stress-induced ER-phagy is the only known selective macroautophagy pathway in S. pombe.
source: In S. pombe, ER stress-induced ER-phagy is the only known selective macroautophagy pathway (Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2020.

claim: DTT-induced processing of Erg11 occurs in a manner dependent on the ER-phagy receptor Epr1.
source: When cells were treated with the ER stress inducer dithiothreitol (DTT), processing of Erg11-CFP occurred in a manner dependent on the ER-phagy receptor Epr1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by Erg11-CFP processing assay data and cites Zhao et al., 2020.

claim: Individually, both Atg1-GFP and Atg1-GBP can complement the autophagy defect of atg1Δ but not atg1Δ atg11Δ.
source: We found that, individually, both Atg1-GFP and Atg1-GBP can complement the autophagy defect of atg1Δ but not atg1Δ atg11Δ (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), indicating that fusing GFP or GBP to Atg1 did not affect its function and either fusion alone cannot bypass Atg11.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data showing vacuolar entry of mCherry-Atg8.

claim: Co-expression of Atg1-GFP and Atg1-GBP rescued the autophagy defect of atg1Δ atg11Δ.
source: As expected, co-expression of Atg1-GFP and Atg1-GBP rescued the autophagy defect of atg1Δ atg11Δ (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Pho8Δ60 assay and fluorescence microscopy data.

claim: The rescue of atg1Δ atg11Δ by co-expression of Atg1-GFP and Atg1-GBP was not affected when kinase-dead mutations were introduced into one but not both subunits.
source: Interestingly, this rescue was not affected when the kinase-dead mutations D193A and T208A were introduced into Atg1-GBP or Atg1-GFP and was only abolished when both Atg1-GFP and Atg1-GBP harbored kinase-dead mutations (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Pho8Δ60 assay and fluorescence microscopy data with kinase-dead mutants.
